cf.title: Proposal to allow setting cursor options on Portals

input.subject: Proposal to allow setting cursor options on Portals

verdict_reasoning: The goal has support in the thread, and the choice of a protocol extension over a version bump is settled. The design of v5 is not: standards-compat-1 shows that negotiating _pq_.cursor changes every Bind and Execute, and the PortalHold alternative from message #52 has no answer. standards-compat-3 and maintenance-fit-2 show that Bind with cursor options and DECLARE already behave differently. already-exists-1 questions whether the Execute fields in 0002 belong in this patch.

brief.title: Cursor options and fetch direction for portals via a protocol extension
brief.problem: Drivers such as pgjdbc cannot create holdable or scrollable portals over the extended query protocol. Today they must rewrite queries into DECLARE CURSOR and FETCH as SQL text, which the author calls cumbersome. A user in the thread reports Java out-of-memory errors when result sets must survive a commit, because the driver then ignores the fetch size.
brief.proposed_design: A new protocol extension, _pq_.cursor, negotiated at startup, adds a mandatory Int32 cursor flags field to every Bind (SCROLL, NO SCROLL, WITH HOLD). It also adds a mandatory Int32 fetch-direction field and an Int64 count to every Execute, so a client can fetch or move as FETCH and MOVE do. libpq gets a connection parameter and new functions to use both.
user_visible_surface: Protocol extension _pq_.cursor, which changes the Bind and Execute message formats on the whole connection once negotiated
libpq functions PQsendExecutePortal and PQsendBindAndExecutePortal, with PQ_FETCH_* constants
libpq trace output prints the new Bind and Execute fields
author_claims: Holdable cursors at protocol level fix an oversight in the original protocol and expose existing server features.
An all-zero Execute trailer behaves byte-for-byte like today's Execute, so drivers that use the row-count field keep working.
Mandatory fields are safer than optional trailers detected by message length when later extensions extend the same message.
Opt-in negotiation avoids adding 4 bytes per Bind and 12 per Execute for clients that do not use cursors.
Everything the patch enables is already possible through SQL today.
brief.thread_state: After a long dispute, Tom Lane, Robert Haas and Jacob Champion favoured a protocol extension over a version bump, and v5 follows that. Sehrope Sarkuni and Vladimir Sitnikov then reported crashes, check gaps, and pooler breakage. Vladimir proposed a separate PortalHold message so that Bind and Execute stay unchanged, and the author has not answered that proposal.
unclear: The material does not show whether the author accepts the fixes in Sehrope's 0004 and 0005 or plans to fold them into v5.
The author has not answered whether HOLD should move to a separate message, as Vladimir proposed, to leave Bind and Execute unchanged for poolers.
The proposal does not say how a pooler in transaction mode can learn that a held portal exists or has been dropped.
The thread does not say whether the Execute fetch fields belong in this patch, given that SQL FETCH can already read a scrollable portal.
The proposal does not say how SCROLL interacts with cached and generic plans, and the planning DECLARE does.

prior_attempts.title: cursors with prepared statements
prior_attempts.quote: I hope it's not another abandoned patch, but due to lack of response I'm marking it as returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.reason: Heikki Linnakangas objected to the USING clause on DECLARE as a non-standard extension and proposed `DECLARE c CURSOR FOR EXECUTE p (foo, bar)` instead. Robert Haas supported the author's syntax, and the discussion stopped in July 2018 with no agreement. After months without activity and no reply to a status inquiry, Dmitry Dolgov marked the entry returned with feedback.
prior_attempts.what_is_different: P1 added SQL syntax to declare a cursor over a prepared statement. This proposal leaves SQL alone and adds cursor options to Bind and fetch fields to Execute through a negotiated protocol extension.

objections.title: Negotiating _pq_.cursor changes every Bind and Execute on the connection
objections.failure_scenario: An application sets protocol_cursor=1 behind PgBouncer 1.22.1 with ignore_startup_parameters = _pq_.cursor. libpq gets no NegotiateProtocolVersion, assumes the option was accepted, and adds the new fields. From then on every extended query on that connection fails with "invalid message format", including queries that never use a cursor.
objections.argument: Message #52 reports this failure and shows that a pooler cannot share a server connection between clients that did and did not negotiate the option. In v5 the fields are mandatory once negotiated, so the cost falls on every Bind and Execute rather than only on messages that use the feature. Message #52 proposes a separate PortalHold message that leaves Bind and Execute unchanged, and the thread has no answer to it. The author's reason for mandatory fields, that length sniffing cannot carry a second extension (message #48), holds just as well for a new message.
objections.author_must_show: Why must holdability travel inside Bind instead of in a separate message, given that only PreCommit_Portals reads CURSOR_OPT_HOLD?

critic.reasoning: Message #52 reports both the PgBouncer 1.22.1 failure and the loss of pool sharing, and the thread has no reply to the PortalHold proposal. The opt-in connection parameter limits who is affected but does not answer why Bind and Execute must change.

objections.title: Protocol cursors do not follow the rules DECLARE applies
objections.failure_scenario: A session with plan_cache_mode = force_generic_plan binds a prepared GROUP BY query with $1 = 0. Without SCROLL it returns 10 rows. With SCROLL the replan folds the parameter in as a constant and Bind fails with division by zero. The same query through DECLARE SCROLL is planned under DECLARE's rules, so the two paths give different results.
objections.argument: v5 crashes on SCROLL for plans that cannot scan backward and on HOLD for non-SELECT portals (message #49). The 0004 fixes then make Bind differ from DECLARE in other ways: it accepts FOR UPDATE with a data-modifying WITH that DECLARE refuses, and it rejects FOR UPDATE in subqueries, CTEs and views that DECLARE accepts (message #51). The documentation says "as for DECLARE", so drivers will rely on a contract that is not met. The material does not show that the author has adopted 0004 or chosen which behaviour is correct.
objections.author_must_show: For which queries and settings does a Bind with SCROLL or HOLD behave the same as DECLARE with the same options, and where does it differ on purpose?

critic.reasoning: Messages #49 and #51 show the crashes in v5 and the remaining differences from DECLARE after 0004. The author has not said whether 0004 is adopted or which behaviour is intended.

objections.title: Second cursor planning and checking path beside DECLARE
objections.failure_scenario: A future patch adds a cursor restriction or planning flag to DECLARE but not to Bind. Clients that use Bind with SCROLL or HOLD then get plans or checks that differ from DECLARE, or hit an executor assertion. Nothing fails at build or test time when the two paths drift.
objections.argument: Message #49 found crashes because Bind reused cached plans not built for backward scans, and allowed HOLD on non-SELECT portals. The fix in 0004 re-plans outside the plan cache. Message #51 shows it still differs from DECLARE in four ways: data-modifying WITH, force_generic_plan, a stricter FOR UPDATE check, and no CURSOR_OPT_FAST_PLAN. Each cursor rule now lives in two places.
objections.author_must_show: Can Bind with cursor options share DECLARE's planning and validation code, so that one rule change covers both paths?

critic.reasoning: Message #51 lists four differences from DECLARE that remain after 0004, so the two paths have already drifted. No message says whether Bind can share DECLARE's planning and checks.

objections.title: Execute fetch fields duplicate SQL FETCH and MOVE on named portals
objections.failure_scenario: Under _pq_.cursor, every driver and pooler must send and parse 12 extra bytes on every Execute to gain what FETCH and MOVE already do. A second fetch path then drifts from SQL FETCH. One case is known: a CALL with an INOUT parameter that commits works through a plain Execute and fails with 2D000 through a directional Execute.
objections.argument: SQL FETCH and MOVE already read a named portal created by Bind in any direction, as message #52 points out, and the author says in message #54 that everything the patch enables is possible through SQL today. The 0002 commit message justifies the fields because only SQL FETCH could scroll, so they save a text query and nothing more. Message #52 lists further defects that exist only because of the second path, such as direction checks running after log_statement.
objections.author_must_show: Which driver task needs a directional Execute that "FETCH BACKWARD n FROM portal" sent over the extended protocol cannot do, apart from saving one query string?

critic.reasoning: A reviewer asked for the Execute fields in message #47, but the author says in message #54 that SQL can do all of it. Nobody in the thread names a task that FETCH on the named portal cannot do, and message #52 reports defects specific to 0002.

objections.title: Bind-time HOLD now covers only what DECLARE WITH HOLD already does
objections.failure_scenario: After 0004, a driver can set HOLD only on a single SELECT, which DECLARE ... WITH HOLD with $n parameters and binary FETCH results already supports. The case SQL cannot do, holding the result of INSERT ... RETURNING across COMMIT, is still rejected. Every Bind on the connection changes format for a gain that the driver could get with SQL.
objections.argument: Message #52 notes that holding a portal at the protocol level is strongest for RETURNING and data-modifying WITH, and that 0004 excludes exactly those. The author's case in messages #1 and #10 is that rewriting queries into DECLARE is cumbersome, which is a matter of convenience rather than a missing capability. The out-of-memory report in message #37 comes from pgjdbc ignoring the fetch size for holdable result sets; DECLARE WITH HOLD plus FETCH avoids that today.
objections.author_must_show: What does a held SELECT portal created by Bind give pgjdbc that DECLARE ... WITH HOLD with parameters and binary FETCH cannot, enough to justify changing every Bind?

critic.reasoning: Several people support the feature, but the stated reason is that the DECLARE rewrite is cumbersome, and DECLARE WITH HOLD can do the SELECT case. The point depends on 0004, which the author has not adopted, but v5 without it crashes on non-SELECT HOLD.

other_surviving.title: Held portals are session state that poolers cannot track
other_surviving.failure_scenario: A pgjdbc client holds portal C_1 through a transaction-mode pooler and commits. The pooler hands the server connection to another client. That client can fetch from C_1, or its own Bind of C_1 fails with 42P03. The first client loses its portal at its next transaction.
other_surviving.argument: Message #52 reports all three effects with a PgBouncer build that forwards the option. A held portal lasts beyond its transaction, but nothing on the wire tells a pooler that one exists or that it was dropped by Close, SQL CLOSE, DISCARD ALL or a failed transaction. The proposal neither adds such a signal nor documents that transaction pooling cannot support HOLD. The thread leaves this open (message #34, message #52).
other_surviving.author_must_show: How does a transaction-mode pooler learn when a held portal is created and when it is gone, or will protocol.sgml state that HOLD is unsupported there?

critic.reasoning: Message #7 notes that SQL-level held cursors have the same limit behind PgBouncer today, so the patch does not create the problem. The open point from message #52 still stands: protocol.sgml does not say that transaction pooling cannot support HOLD.

refuted.title: Execute fetch fields duplicate FETCH and give Execute a second meaning
refuted.failure_scenario: A driver moves a plain Execute loop to PQsendExecutePortal with FORWARD and count 0, as the row count of a plain Execute allows. It gets the current row again, not all rows. Separately, a procedure with an INOUT parameter that commits runs through plain Execute but fails with 2D000 through Execute with FORWARD ALL.
refuted.argument: SQL FETCH and MOVE can already read a scrollable portal by name in any direction (message #52), and the author says everything here is already possible in SQL (message #54). v5-0002 adds a second row count to Execute whose zero means the opposite of the existing field. Message #52 also reports that a directional Execute runs portals with a different isTopLevel than a plain Execute does. So one message gets two behaviour sets that drivers must keep apart.
refuted.author_must_show: What can a client do with the Execute fields in 0002 that SQL FETCH and MOVE on the same named portal cannot do?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1. Its one separate point, that count 0 re-fetches the current row, copies FETCH FORWARD 0 and the libpq documentation in 0003 states it.

refuted.title: Negotiating _pq_.cursor changes every Bind and Execute on the connection
refuted.failure_scenario: A pooler in transaction mode serves one client that negotiated _pq_.cursor and one that did not. Their Bind and Execute messages now have different formats, so the pooler cannot share a server connection between them. The operator learns this when the pooler needs separate pools or starts rewriting messages.
refuted.argument: In v5, once the option is negotiated, every Bind carries 4 extra bytes and every Execute carries 12, including messages from code that never uses a cursor option (message #48, 0001 and 0002 commit messages). Message #52 proposes a separate PortalHold message, plus a Bind variant if SCROLL stays, so that Bind and Execute stay unchanged. The author has not replied to that. Message #28 describes a proxy that parses the whole Bind message, so the format change reaches real middleboxes.
refuted.author_must_show: Why must the new fields live inside Bind and Execute rather than in separate messages that leave both formats unchanged for poolers?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which makes the same pool-sharing point and asks the same question about separate messages.

refuted.title: A dropped _pq_.cursor parameter breaks every extended query
refuted.failure_scenario: An older pooler is set to ignore _pq_.cursor and does not send NegotiateProtocolVersion. libpq assumes the option was accepted and appends the new fields, and the server rejects every Bind as "invalid message format". Message #52 shows this with psql "select $1 \bind 42 \g" through PgBouncer 1.22.1.
refuted.argument: The 0001 commit message says libpq disables the feature only when NegotiateProtocolVersion rejects it, so silence counts as acceptance. Because the fields are mandatory on every message, a wrong guess breaks every parameterized query and not only cursor use. With a separate message, the same mistake would break only the new message (message #52).
refuted.author_must_show: How does a client confirm the server accepted _pq_.cursor before changing all Bind and Execute formats, when a middlebox drops the parameter without NegotiateProtocolVersion?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1, which uses the same PgBouncer 1.22.1 scenario. Treating a missing NegotiateProtocolVersion as acceptance is how `_pq_.` options are defined, so only the size of the breakage is specific to this patch.

refuted.title: Held portals become readable by other clients behind a transaction pooler
refuted.failure_scenario: A multi-tenant application runs behind a transaction-mode pooler, and its RLS policies read a per-transaction setting. pgjdbc opens a holdable result set for tenant A as portal C_1, which outlives the transaction. Tenant B gets the same server connection, fetches from its own C_1, and receives tenant A's rows. Nobody notices, because no error is raised.
refuted.argument: Message #52 reports that, through a patched PgBouncer, another client could fetch from the held portal, and that a name collision on C_1 occurred. SQL DECLARE WITH HOLD has the same exposure, but there the application chooses the cursor name. Under this proposal a driver turns standard JDBC holdability into held portals with predictable names, so cross-client reads become accidental rather than deliberate. The author has not answered message #52, and the proposal gives a pooler no way to learn when a held portal exists or has been dropped.
refuted.author_must_show: How does a transaction-mode pooler learn that a held portal exists and has been dropped, or will protocol.sgml state that such poolers must refuse _pq_.cursor HOLD?

critic.reasoning: Message #52 reports that the next client's Bind of C_1 fails with 42P03, so a driver that binds before it fetches gets an error, not another tenant's rows. The pooler side of this is covered by replication-ondisk-3, and DECLARE WITH HOLD has the same exposure today.

refuted.title: Whole-connection Bind and Execute format change does not accumulate well
refuted.failure_scenario: A pooler serves clients with and without _pq_.cursor, so it must keep separate server pools or rewrite every Bind and Execute. A later extension that also appends to Bind doubles the pool variants again. Each driver, pooler and libpq encoder must emit the new fields on every message, including code that never uses a cursor.
refuted.argument: v5 makes the fields mandatory on every Bind and Execute once negotiated (0001, 0002 commit messages). Message #52 shows PgBouncer 1.22 failing every extended query when it drops the option, and pool sharing is lost. In messages #24 and #32 Robert worried about many small protocol tweaks. Ten such extensions per release, each changing the core message layout, would be hard on the ecosystem. Message #52 proposes a separate PortalHold message, and the thread has no reply to it.
refuted.author_must_show: Why must holdability change the format of every Bind and Execute rather than travel in a separate message such as the PortalHold one proposed in message #52?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of standards-compat-1. The added accumulation argument rests on later extensions that the material does not show.

refuted.title: Execute fetch fields duplicate SQL FETCH and widen the patch
refuted.failure_scenario: Every Execute that libpq or a driver builds carries 12 extra bytes once negotiated. A directional Execute adds new behaviours, such as isTopLevel handling for CALL, PortalSuspended rules and error ordering. Message #52 reports bugs in each of these.
refuted.argument: SQL FETCH and MOVE can already read a scrollable named portal in any direction, as message #52 notes. The 0002 commit message says the Execute fields are there to make SCROLL useful, but FETCH already does that. Message #54 states that everything the patch enables is possible through SQL today. The added protocol surface and four new libpq exports must be kept forever, and the benefit is avoiding a FETCH statement.
refuted.author_must_show: What does a directional Execute let a driver do that SQL FETCH on the same named portal cannot do, and is that worth making it part of this first patch?

refuted.title: HOLD limited to SELECT matches what DECLARE WITH HOLD already gives
refuted.failure_scenario: pgjdbc adopts _pq_.cursor for holdable result sets. Users behind transaction-mode poolers lose the portal at the next transaction, or another client reads it, as message #52 reports. The driver still needs the DECLARE fallback for older servers and for poolers that decline the option.
refuted.argument: After 0004, HOLD works only for a single SELECT, and DECLARE ... WITH HOLD already covers that case (message #52). The one real gap, holding RETURNING results, is deferred. The out-of-memory report in message #37 comes from the driver ignoring fetch size, and a driver using DECLARE could fix it. Drivers keep the SQL path either way, so core takes on a permanent protocol surface without removing driver code.
refuted.author_must_show: Which user problem can pgjdbc fix with protocol-level HOLD on a SELECT portal but not with DECLARE WITH HOLD, given that it needs the DECLARE fallback anyway?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-2. Its failure scenario about poolers is covered by replication-ondisk-3.

refuted.title: Fetch direction on Execute has no user asking for it
refuted.failure_scenario: A driver enables _pq_.cursor to get WITH HOLD. From then on, every Execute it sends must carry 12 extra bytes, and every pooler and proxy in the path must parse them, though the driver never scrolls. A pooler that does not parse them breaks every extended query on that connection, as message #52 shows.
refuted.argument: The only request for Execute fetch fields came from a reviewer who wanted the feature to be complete (message #47). No user in the thread asks to scroll over the wire. Message #52 notes that SQL FETCH and MOVE can already read a scrollable portal by name, and message #54 confirms all of this is possible through SQL today. 0002 brings its own new problems, such as CALL with isTopLevel = false (message #52), and these costs fall on every connection that negotiates the extension.
refuted.author_must_show: Which driver or application needs backward or absolute fetch over Execute, and why does SQL FETCH on the named portal not serve it?

critic.reasoning: Duplicate of already-exists-1. Its pooler scenario is covered by standards-compat-1.

refuted.title: HOLD limited to a single SELECT only duplicates DECLARE WITH HOLD
refuted.failure_scenario: pgjdbc moves holdable result sets to the protocol path. After 0004, HOLD on INSERT ... RETURNING or on a data-modifying WITH is rejected at Bind. The driver must keep its DECLARE fallback for SELECT anyway, and the statements that SQL cannot hold stay unsolved.
refuted.argument: The concrete field report in message #37 is a large SELECT that must survive COMMIT, and DECLARE ... WITH HOLD already handles that. The author's reason for a protocol path is that query rewriting is "cumbersome" (message #1). Message #52 says the only case SQL cannot cover is RETURNING and data-modifying WITH, which 0004 excludes and leaves as a follow-up. So the version under review adds a new wire format mainly to spare drivers a rewrite they can already do.
refuted.author_must_show: For SELECT, what does a protocol-level HOLD give pgjdbc users that DECLARE WITH HOLD does not, measured in failures or lost performance?

touch_points.label: wire protocol
touch_points.reason: _pq_.cursor adds a mandatory Int32 to every Bind and an Int32 plus Int64 to every Execute once negotiated.

touch_points.label: ABI / extension API
touch_points.reason: exports.txt gains four libpq functions, and libpq-fe.h gains the PQ_FETCH_* constants.

touch_points.label: SQL-standard conflict or non-standard syntax
touch_points.reason: see objection standards-compat-3: Protocol cursors do not follow the rules DECLARE applies

touch_points.label: planner behaviour change
touch_points.reason: A Bind with SCROLL needs a plan that can scan backward, so it cannot reuse a cached plan as is (messages #49, #51).

touch_points.label: security / privileges
touch_points.reason: A held portal outlives its transaction, so behind a transaction-mode pooler another client can reach it (message #52).

touch_points.label: maintenance burden ("who maintains this in 10 years")
touch_points.reason: The patch adds a permanent wire format, four libpq exports, and a second cursor checking path beside DECLARE.

touch_points.label: performance on the hot path
touch_points.reason: exec_bind_message and the Execute path in postgres.c read extra fields, but only on connections that negotiated the option.

touch_points.label: doesn't fit what Postgres is about (extension / external tool / already solved)
touch_points.reason: The author states in message #54 that SQL DECLARE, FETCH and MOVE already provide everything the patch enables.

questions: Why must holdability travel inside Bind, and not in a separate message such as the PortalHold proposed in message #52, which leaves Bind and Execute unchanged?
Which driver task needs a directional Execute that SQL FETCH or MOVE on the same named portal cannot do, apart from saving one query string?
Will Sehrope's 0004 and 0005 be folded into the next version, and if so, which of the remaining differences from DECLARE listed in message #51 are intended?
Can Bind with SCROLL or HOLD share DECLARE's planning and validation code, so that one rule change covers both paths?
How does a transaction-mode pooler learn that a held portal exists or is gone, or will protocol.sgml state that HOLD is unsupported there?

committability.owner_note: It needs a committer who knows the extended query protocol, portal and plan cache code in tcop, and libpq. Tom Lane, Robert Haas and Jacob Champion joined only the negotiation debate, not the v5 design.
committability.liability: The owner signs for a wire format and four libpq exports that cannot be removed. The owner also signs for every later difference between Bind and DECLARE, and for pooler breakage reports.
committability.author_follow_up: The author posted v5 in message #48, replied in message #54 and moved the entry across CommitFests. The PortalHold proposal and the 0004 and 0005 fixes have no answer yet.

priority.reason: Demand comes from JDBC holdable result sets, postgres_fdw interest and one out-of-memory field report. The series is about 100 KiB across postgres.c, backend_startup.c and libpq, and it fixes a wire format, so the open design question from message #52 should be settled before code review.

provisional_note: Without the code, the crash fixes in 0004 and 0005 and the reported isTopLevel difference for a directional Execute could not be checked. The review saw only 3 of 54 messages in full, so later thread facts come from the panel's reports.
disclosure: Prepared by an AI harness; treat as a devil's advocate, not a verdict.

precedents_retrieved.title: cursors with prepared statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch adds `DECLARE cursor_name CURSOR FOR prepared_statement_name [ USING param, ... ]` so a cursor can be declared over a prepared statement. It attaches USING to DECLARE because direct SQL has no OPEN command, and it changes the ECPG parser to override the new main-parser rules.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Heikki Linnakangas objected to the USING clause on DECLARE as a non-standard extension and proposed `DECLARE c CURSOR FOR EXECUTE p (foo, bar)` instead. Robert Haas supported the author's syntax, and the discussion stopped in July 2018 with no agreement. After months without activity and no reply to a status inquiry, Dmitry Dolgov marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
I hope it's not another abandoned patch, but due to lack of response I'm
marking it as returned with feedback.

precedents_retrieved.title: loop over unbound cursor
precedents_retrieved.summary: Allow the PL/pgSQL FOR loop to iterate over an unbound refcursor that was opened earlier, in addition to bound cursors. If the FOR statement opened the portal itself it closes it at loop end; otherwise iteration continues over the already-open portal, so one cursor can be read across several loops.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Tom Lane saw no gain over a plain FOR-over-SELECT and thought splitting one iteration across two loops encourages poor programming practice. He also objected that a FOR loop which may or may not own its cursor loses a self-contained definition of its iterations and is no cleaner than a hand-built loop around FETCH. The author replied with use cases (refcursors passed as arguments, symmetry with FETCH, dbms_sql patterns), and the entry was withdrawn with no further messages.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote:
The point of a FOR loop, IMO, is to have a fairly self-contained
definition of the set of iterations that will occur.  This
eliminates that property, leaving you with something no cleaner
than a hand-built loop around a FETCH command.

precedents_retrieved.title: PARALLEL flag for cursors
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a PARALLEL option to DECLARE CURSOR so that user-defined cursors can use parallel plans, which Postgres disables for them today. The existing ban on DML during parallel mode stays, and workers stay assigned to the cursor while it is suspended.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas said a suspended parallel cursor is a hard problem with no design yet. Keeping workers alive would need state such as new combo CIDs sent to them, and errors would leave group locking out of step. Locking out every command except FETCH is very limiting, and the patch does not say how a worker error is reported while the leader is idle. David Steele returned the patch because the discussion of how it should work was still going on, and it never had a code-level review.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: Say the worker hits an error while the leader is idle; how do we report the error?

precedents_retrieved.title: Add new protocol message to change GUCs to be able to change protocol extension parameters
precedents_retrieved.summary: Add a protocol message that lets a client set a GUC without a SET command, so poolers can see the change and some parameters can be set only at the protocol level. Over time the work became a patch set with a protocol minor version bump, min_protocol_version and max_protocol_version libpq options, and protocol parameters such as report_parameters.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author withdrew the entry and moved the remaining protocol patches to the thread about longer cancel keys. Some pieces were committed here, including a libpq function PQfullProtocolVersion added in place of redefining PQprotocolVersion. The visible messages show no objection that rejected the core design.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: This required another rebase, but I've decided that I think it'll be most fruitful to continue the discussion on protocol changes in the thread about longer cancel keys[1].

precedents_retrieved.title: Use "protocol options" name instead of "protocol extensions" everywhere
precedents_retrieved.objectors: Heikki Linnakangas, Robert Haas, Jacob Champion, Laurenz Albe, Peter Eisentraut
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch replaces the term "protocol extensions" with "protocol options" in the docs and in a libpq error message, because "extension" suggests a link to Postgres extensions. No protocol options existed yet, so the author saw this as the time to settle on one name.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Reviewers did not agree on a new name. Heikki Linnakangas said "protocol option" suggests GUCs, Robert Haas found "protocol extensions" mildly clearer, Jacob Champion preferred keeping "protocol extension" with a docs note, and Laurenz Albe voted to keep "extension" because "option" already names other things in the docs. Peter Eisentraut rejected the patch for lack of consensus to change.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't think there is consensus for change, so I'm rejecting it.

precedents_retrieved.title: Improve cursor handling in pg_stat_statements
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch changes pg_stat_statements so that DECLARE CURSOR statements are normalized, get a queryId and have their planning time tracked. Execution statistics are then counted under the DECLARE CURSOR entry instead of under FETCH, and CLOSE is no longer tracked.
precedents_retrieved.objection: The visible messages do not show why. Only the author's opening message is shown, with no replies, and the entry was withdrawn about four weeks later.

precedents_retrieved.title: Revert "Add GUC checks for ssl_min_protocol_version and ssl_max_protocol_version"
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Add GUC checks for ssl_min_protocol_version and ssl_max_protocol_version"
Reverted commit(s): Add GUC checks for ssl_min_protocol_version and ssl_max_protocol_version
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 41aadee, as the GUC checks could run on older values
with the new values used, and result in incorrect errors if both
parameters are changed at the same time.

Per complaint from Tom Lane.

precedents_retrieved.title: temporary file usage report with extended protocol and unnamed portals
precedents_retrieved.summary: With the extended protocol, the log_temp_files message for an unnamed portal is attributed to the next query, because the portal and its temporary file are dropped only when the next Bind arrives. The patches either drop the unnamed portal as soon as it runs to completion (Sami's v4/v5) or drop a pre-existing unnamed portal before debug_query_string is set (v3, v6).
precedents_retrieved.objection: The author found that v5, which drops the unnamed portal right after execution, conflicts with the protocol documentation, which says an unnamed portal lives until the end of the transaction or the next Bind to it. The v6 alternative follows the protocol but logs no query at all in some cases. The author saw no clean way to get correct logging, and the entry was withdrawn. Earlier, Sami Imseih noted that v3 read queryDesc->sourceText in DropPortal, though mmgr/README says the query string may not live as long as the portal.

precedents_retrieved.summary:
Revert "Drop unnamed portal immediately after execution to completion"

precedents_retrieved.objection:
This reverts commit 1fd981f05369, based on concerns that the logging
improvements do not justify the protocol breakage of dropping an unnamed
portal once its execution has completed.

It seems unlikely that one would try to send an execute or describe
message after the portal has been used, but if they do such
post-completion messages would not be able to process as the previous
versions.  Let's revert this change for now so as we keep compatibility
and consider a different solution.

The tests added by 76bba033128a track the pre-1fd981f05369 behavior, and
are still valid.

precedents_retrieved.title: Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Rearrange execution of PARAM_EXTERN Params for plpgsql's benefit.
Reverted commit(s): Further reduce overhead for passing plpgsql variables to the executor.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
This patch does three interrelated things:

* Create a new expression execution step type EEOP_PARAM_CALLBACK
and add the infrastructure needed for add-on modules to generate that.
As discussed, the best control mechanism for that seems to be to add
another hook function to ParamListInfo, which will be called by
ExecInitExpr if it's supplied and a PARAM_EXTERN Param is found.
For stand-alone expressions, we add a new entry point to allow the
ParamListInfo to be specified directly, since it can't be retrieved
from the parent plan node's EState.

* Redesign the API for the ParamListInfo paramFetch hook so that the
ParamExternData array can be entirely virtual.  This also lets us get rid
of ParamListInfo.paramMask, instead leaving it to the paramFetch hook to
decide which param IDs should be accessible or not.  plpgsql_param_fetch
was already doing the identical masking check, so having callers do it too
seemed redundant.  While I was at it, I added a "speculative" flag to
paramFetch that the planner can specify as TRUE to avoid unwanted failures.
This solves an ancient problem for plpgsql that it couldn't provide values
of non-DTYPE_VAR variables to the planner for fear of triggering premature
"record not assigned yet" or "field not found" errors during planning.

* Rework plpgsql to get rid of the need for "unshared" parameter lists,
by dint of turning the single ParamListInfo per estate into a nearly
read-only data structure that doesn't instantiate any per-variable data.
Instead, the paramFetch hook controls access to per-variable data and can
make the right decisions on the fly, replacing the cases that we used to
need multiple ParamListInfos for.  This might perhaps have been a
performance loss on its own, but by using a paramCompile hook we can
bypass plpgsql_param_fetch entirely during normal query execution.
(It's now only called when, eg, we copy the ParamListInfo into a cursor
portal.  copyParamList() or SerializeParamList() effectively instantiate
the virtual parameter array as a simple physical array without a
paramFetch hook, which is what we want in those cases.)  This allows
reverting most of commit 6c82d8d1f, though I kept the cosmetic
code-consolidation aspects of that (eg the assign_simple_var function).

Performance testing shows this to be at worst a break-even change,
and it can provide wins ranging up to 20% in test cases involving
accesses to fields of "record" variables.  The fact that values of
such variables can now be exposed to the planner might produce wins
in some situations, too, but I've not pursued that angle.

In passing, remove the "parent" pointer from the arguments to
ExecInitExprRec and related functions, instead storing that pointer in a
transient field in ExprState.  The ParamListInfo pointer for a stand-alone
expression is handled the same way; we'd otherwise have had to add
yet another recursively-passed-down argument in expression compilation.

precedents_retrieved.title: Password identifiers, protocol aging and SCRAM protocol
precedents_retrieved.summary: The patch set moves password storage from pg_authid into a new pg_auth_verifiers catalog, allowing one verifier per protocol per role, with a superuser GUC (password_protocols) and a sanitize function used by pg_upgrade to retire outdated protocols. On top of this it adds refactoring patches and SCRAM-SHA1 authentication as a new password protocol.
precedents_retrieved.objection: Robert Haas argued that the work should move to the next release cycle: these are large, user-facing changes involving wire protocol changes, and they had received little detailed code-level review. He judged that they could not be completed safely in the three weeks before feature freeze, and he questioned whether there was consensus on the direction, including multiple password verifiers. The author agreed that the SCRAM patch (0009) needed more time than remained, and no committer took it on; Magnus Hagander said he lacked time in this CommitFest. The author marked the entry returned with feedback.
precedents_retrieved.key_quote: I don't see how we're going to get all of this into 9.6, and these are big, user-facing changes that I don't think we should rush into under time pressure.

precedents_retrieved.title: Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
precedents_retrieved.summary:
Fix index-only scan plans, take 2.
Reverted commit(s): Fix index-only scan plans when not all index columns can be returned.
precedents_retrieved.objection:
Commit 4ace45677 failed to fix the problem fully, because the
same issue of attempting to fetch a non-returnable index column
can occur when rechecking the indexqual after using a lossy index
operator.  Moreover, it broke EXPLAIN for such indexquals (which
indicates a gap in our test cases :-().

Revert the code changes of 4ace45677 in favor of adding a new field
to struct IndexOnlyScan, containing a version of the indexqual that
can be executed against the index-returned tuple without using any
non-returnable columns.  (The restrictions imposed by check_index_only
guarantee this is possible, although we may have to recompute indexed
expressions.)  Support construction of that during setrefs.c
processing by marking IndexOnlyScan.indextlist entries as resjunk
if they can't be returned, rather than removing them entirely.
(We could alternatively require setrefs.c to look up the IndexOptInfo
again, but abusing resjunk this way seems like a reasonably safe way
to avoid needing to do that.)

This solution isn't great from an API-stability standpoint: if there
are any extensions out there that build IndexOnlyScan structs directly,
they'll be broken in the next minor releases.  However, only a very
invasive extension would be likely to do such a thing.  There's no
change in the Path representation, so typical planner extensions
shouldn't have a problem.

As before, back-patch to all supported branches.

roaster_notes.note: No listed precedent records a reason that applies here: P1 stalled on syntax and inactivity, and P4, P9 and P21 concern other protocol changes. The thread already replaced its own first design, a 3.3 version bump (message #1), with _pq_.cursor after messages #20, #24 and #29, so that question is settled.
Objections found; the move from a version bump to a protocol extension was settled in the thread (messages #20 to #35), so it is not raised.
The proposal changes no on-disk format, WAL or catalog. Its persistent effects are in the wire protocol and in session state for held portals, and the objections cover those.

Apart from pooler session state, the extension only exposes cursor options that SQL already grants to every role, and it adds no new privilege. Sehrope's 0004 fixes the crash and overflow cases. Their correctness cannot be checked without the code.
Objections listed. On committability, no committer has engaged with v5. Tom, Robert and Jacob took part only in the negotiation debate.
Both objections rest on SQL DECLARE, FETCH and MOVE, which already provide the capability. Neither says the protocol gap is imaginary.

Demand for protocol-level WITH HOLD is shown: the JDBC holdable result set API (message #1), postgres_fdw interest (message #2), and one company's out-of-memory reports (messages #37, #50). The objections concern the Execute scope and the SELECT-only limit.
